messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Sister Elena is a 44-year-old nun who came to the clinic at the insistence of her Mother Superior, who had noticed her growing isolation and distress. The traumatic event that shattered her life occurred three years ago, when a terrorist bomb exploded inside her convent’s chapel during morning Mass. Elena was in the front row, kneeling; the blast threw her against a stone pillar. She came to lying in a pool of blood—not her own, but that of a novice who had been beside her and was killed instantly. The scene seared into her: the heat, the screams, the acrid smoke, and the sight of crimson spreading across the white floor. In the months that followed, she was diagnosed with a chronic lower back injury from the impact, and she carried a deep, unspoken guilt about surviving.

The first symptoms were subtle. Elena began waking from nightmares in which she was back in that chapel—she could hear the ringing, feel the debris hitting her skin. The dream residue, a lingering sense of unreality, would persist for hours, making her feel unsafe even in her own cell. At the same time, any sharp physical pain in her back would immediately flood her with the same overwhelming fear and horror she had felt that morning. The pain became a trigger that seemed to unlock the entire traumatic memory uncontrollably, as if her body were reliving the moment. She found that when she tried to deliberately recall what happened—to piece it together for the police or for her own understanding—the details were fragmented and hazy, yet the memory would force its way into her mind unbidden, complete with the full sensory onslaught: the smell, the sound, the sight of blood.

Elena started to avoid what she could. Crowded places like the town market became unbearable; she would see a crowd and immediately feel her chest tighten with fear, and she would retreat to the convent. More subtly, she began avoiding emotional intimacy with her fellow sisters. She had come to believe that getting close to anyone meant risking another loss, and that the only way to be safe was to stay distant. When she did allow herself to be with others, her mind would go over and over the details of the bombing, trying to make sense of why it happened and why she survived—a loop of analysis that only deepened her shame and grief. This overanalyzing did not bring clarity; it intensified her threat perception, making her feel that danger lurked everywhere.

Over time, Elena became convinced that safety existed only inside her own room and the chapel, and that anywhere else required constant vigilance. She always scanned for escape routes before she could feel comfortable in a room, even in the convent’s refectory. The need to plan exits was so strong that it kept her hyperaware of her body, and then the physical pain from her back would spike, pulling her back into threat mode. Her world narrowed: she stopped attending community events, stopped going to the local clinic for fear of seeing blood, and stopped talking to the younger nuns who reached out to her. She became certain that the only way to control her fear was to control her environment completely.

But the cost was high. Her Mother Superior noticed that Elena rarely left her room and seemed hollowed out. In the last months, Elena found herself unable to sleep for more than a few hours; the nightmares returned every night. She finally agreed to seek help when she realized she could not even enter the chapel without planning escape routes and feeling a wave of negative emotions. What frightened her most was the thought that she might never be able to feel at peace again—that the blood and the guilt would always follow her, no matter how many doors she locked.
